A senior Taliban commander, Mohammed Ibrahim Hanafi, has issued alarming threats against foreign aid workers operating in Afghanistan, stating that they could be executed as spies or held as bargaining chips to secure the release of imprisoned Taliban fighters. These threats are reportedly grounded in the group's newly established "constitution," which appears to grant militant commanders broad authority to target humanitarian personnel under the guise of national security concerns. This development raises serious questions about the safety of international aid organizations continuing to operate within the country.

Compounding these concerns, reports indicate that the Taliban's intelligence apparatus has been actively engaged in surveillance operations, systematically gathering information on foreign aid workers throughout Afghanistan. This intelligence-gathering effort suggests a coordinated strategy that could serve as groundwork for future detentions, expulsions, or acts of violence against humanitarian staff, further complicating the already precarious operating environment for international relief efforts in the region.

On the domestic front, Hanafi reaffirmed the Taliban's steadfast commitment to barring girls from public education. He articulated the group's ideological justification for this policy, asserting that women preserve their honor and dignity by remaining in the domestic sphere rather than pursuing education or employment outside the home. This rhetoric reflects a broader worldview that positions women's societal roles as fundamentally confined to the private, familial domain.

Reinforcing the continuity of this hardline stance, Hanafi explicitly stated that the Taliban continues to adhere to the same legal framework established during Mullah Mohammad Omar's original rule in the 1990s. This declaration underscores the group's resistance to reform despite international pressure and shifting global expectations, signaling that the current Taliban administration remains ideologically anchored to its historical precedent rather than adapting to contemporary human rights standards.

The consequences of these policies have manifested in increasingly violent forms. Acid attacks and other forms of violence targeting girls who attempt to attend school have surged, creating an atmosphere of fear that has contributed to the failure of more than 600 schools to open this academic year. Despite this escalating danger, many young students have demonstrated remarkable resilience and determination, continuing to pursue their education against significant personal risk—a testament to their unwavering commitment to learning even as the Taliban's restrictive policies and the violence they inspire threaten to extinguish these educational aspirations entirely.

# Taliban Threatens Foreign Aid Workers Amid Crackdown on Girls' Education

In an exclusive interview with CNN, a senior Taliban commander revealed disturbing new policies that underscore the group's escalating campaign of intimidation across Afghanistan. Mohammed Ibrahim Hanafi, speaking on behalf of the Taliban's emerging governance structure, disclosed that under what the group is calling its new "constitution," foreign aid workers operating in Taliban-controlled areas could face execution if deemed to be spies, or potentially be used as bargaining chips to secure the release of captured Taliban fighters.

The revelation raises serious concerns for the safety of international humanitarian personnel working in some of Afghanistan's most dangerous and remote regions, where aid organizations have long struggled to balance their mission of providing critical assistance with the ever-present threat of violence from insurgent groups.

Hanafi's comments came as he also reaffirmed the Taliban's continued adherence to its notorious ban on education for girls, a policy that harkens back to the group's brutal rule in the late 1990s. Under those old rules, girls were forbidden from attending school beyond a certain age, effectively cutting off an entire generation of Afghan women from formal education and, by extension, from future economic and social opportunities.

This latest confirmation of the Taliban's stance comes at a particularly alarming moment, as it coincides with a disturbing wave of violent attacks targeting schoolgirls across Afghanistan. These attacks have included brutal acid assaults on young girls simply attempting to attend classes, part of a broader pattern of intimidation aimed at discouraging families from allowing their daughters to pursue an education. The violence has had a chilling effect nationwide, forcing more than 600 schools to shut their doors entirely, leaving countless students without access to education and deepening the educational crisis in a country already struggling with widespread illiteracy and limited opportunities for women.

The convergence of these threats—against both foreign humanitarian workers and Afghan schoolgirls—paints a stark picture of the dangers facing anyone who challenges the Taliban's rigid ideological framework. Aid workers, who often serve as a lifeline for vulnerable communities in conflict-affected areas, now face the possibility of being treated as enemy combatants or hostages rather than neutral humanitarian actors. Meanwhile, young Afghan girls who dare to seek an education, along with their families and teachers who support them, continue to risk violent retaliation simply for pursuing basic human rights that are guaranteed under international law.

Human rights organizations and international observers have expressed growing alarm at these developments, warning that the Taliban's actions represent a significant setback for both humanitarian access and gender equality in Afghanistan. The situation highlights the precarious balance that aid organizations must navigate as they attempt to continue their critical work in the country, even as the Taliban's territorial control expands and its enforcement of hardline policies intensifies.

As the international community watches these developments unfold, questions remain about how humanitarian organizations will respond to these explicit threats, and whether continued operations in Taliban-controlled territories remain feasible given the escalating risks. For Afghan girls and their families, the message from the Taliban remains unequivocal: access to education will continue to be met with violence, intimidation, and the enforcement of policies that strip away fundamental rights, regardless of international condemnation or pressure for reform.

# Kabul: A City Shaped by History and Conflict

Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, has long stood at the crossroads of history, culture, and geopolitics. Nestled in a valley surrounded by the Hindu Kush mountains, the city has served as a vital hub for trade and cultural exchange for centuries, connecting South Asia, Central Asia, and the Middle East.

In recent decades, Kabul has become synonymous with conflict and transformation. Following the withdrawal of international forces in 2021 and the subsequent takeover by the Taliban, the city has experienced dramatic shifts in its political, social, and humanitarian landscape. International media outlets, including CNN, have played a crucial role in documenting these changes, providing global audiences with on-the-ground reporting about the daily lives of Kabul's residents, the challenges faced by women and girls under new restrictions, and the broader humanitarian crisis affecting the country.

CNN's coverage of Afghanistan has often highlighted the resilience of the Afghan people amid economic hardship, political uncertainty, and security concerns. Journalists reporting from Kabul have captured stories ranging from the struggles of ordinary families to the complex diplomatic negotiations involving international aid and recognition of the Taliban government.

Despite the hardships, Kabul remains a city of deep cultural significance, home to historic sites, bustling markets, and a population that continues to navigate an uncertain future. The international community's attention, often channeled through outlets like CNN, continues to shape global understanding of Afghanistan's evolving situation, underscoring the importance of continued dialogue, humanitarian support, and awareness of the human stories behind the headlines.

Kabul's story is far from over—it remains a city defined by both its turbulent past and the unwavering spirit of its people.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a Taliban commander threatening to kill or kidnap foreign aid workers in Afghanistan, citing a new "constitution."
counterfactuals.output:
**Taliban Commander Threatens Foreign Aid Workers, Cites Unrecognized "New Constitution"**

*By CNN Staff*

KABUL, Afghanistan — A regional Taliban commander has issued explicit threats against international humanitarian workers operating in Afghanistan, warning that foreign nationals could face kidnapping or death if they fail to comply with a document he described as the group's "new constitution" — a text that has not been publicly released, ratified through any recognized process, or acknowledged by international bodies.

The threats, which emerged through statements circulated in the commander's home province and corroborated by two aid organizations operating in the region, have sent a chill through the humanitarian community already navigating a precarious operating environment under Taliban rule.

"We were told that our foreign staff must either leave or submit to new rules under this so-called constitution, or face consequences — kidnapping, or worse," said a security officer for an international NGO who spoke to CNN on condition of anonymity, citing safety concerns for staff still in the country.

The commander, whose name CNN is withholding pending independent verification of his current operational authority, reportedly made the statements to local elders and was relayed to aid groups through informal channels rather than any formal Taliban government communication. The Taliban's central leadership in Kabul has not commented on the threats, and it remains unclear whether the statements reflect broader policy or represent a unilateral move by a local commander.

Afghanistan analysts caution that such fragmented messaging is not unusual within the Taliban movement, which has struggled to present a unified command structure since retaking power in August 2021.

"The Taliban is not a monolith," said Fatima Gailani, a former Afghan diplomat and analyst on regional security issues. "You have commanders in the provinces who operate with significant autonomy, and sometimes their rhetoric — or their threats — do not reflect the official position of the leadership in Kabul. That doesn't make the threats less dangerous for the people on the ground."

The purported "new constitution" has not been shared with the United Nations, foreign governments, or major press outlets, raising questions about its authenticity and legal weight. The Taliban's de facto government has previously governed largely through edicts issued by its supreme leader, Haibatullah Akhundzada, rather than a codified constitutional framework, making the sudden invocation of such a document unusual.

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said it was "aware of concerning reports" and was seeking clarification through its channels with Taliban authorities in Kabul.

"Any threat against humanitarian personnel is unacceptable," a UNAMA spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. "Humanitarian workers are in Afghanistan solely to provide life-saving assistance to the Afghan people, and their safety must be guaranteed."

Aid organizations, many of which provide critical food, medical, and shelter assistance to millions of Afghans amid a dire economic and humanitarian crisis, now face agonizing decisions about whether to scale back operations or withdraw foreign staff altogether.

"Every time something like this happens, it's the Afghan people who suffer the most," said one Kabul-based humanitarian coordinator. "If foreign workers pull out, entire programs can collapse — clean water projects, malnutrition clinics, emergency food distribution. We are trying to assess the credibility of the threat without abandoning the communities we serve."

This is not the first time foreign aid workers have been targeted in Afghanistan since the Taliban takeover. Previous incidents, including detentions and, in isolated cases, violent attacks, have prompted several organizations to reduce international staffing and rely more heavily on local personnel — though local staff face their own set of risks, particularly women, who have faced sweeping restrictions on their ability to work for NGOs.

The State Department and several European foreign ministries said they were monitoring the situation closely. A U.S. official, speaking on background, said Washington had no independent confirmation of the "new constitution" but was "taking any threat to aid workers seriously."

CNN has reached out to the Taliban's Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment but had not received a response at the time of publication.

The incident underscores the fragile and often contradictory nature of governance in Afghanistan nearly four years after the Taliban's return to power, where international engagement remains limited, humanitarian access is tenuous, and the rule of law — let alone any singular legal document — remains an open and contested question.

*CNN's Kabul bureau contributed to this report. Some sources' identities have been withheld due to security concerns.*

# Taliban Threats Against Aid Workers Escalate as Girls' Education Ban Continues

**KABUL** — Humanitarian organizations operating in Afghanistan report a marked increase in threats and intimidation from Taliban officials in recent weeks, even as the ban on girls' secondary education stretches into its third year with no sign of reversal.

Several aid workers, speaking on condition of anonymity due to fears for their safety, described visits from local Taliban officials demanding changes to hiring practices, program content, and staff composition. Two international NGOs said they had received explicit warnings that continued employment of female staff in certain roles could result in the revocation of operating licenses.

"We are trying to deliver food and medicine to people who have nothing," said one aid coordinator with an international organization working in eastern Afghanistan. "Instead we spend half our time negotiating for our own safety and the safety of our colleagues."

The threats come as the United Nations and humanitarian partners struggle to meet the needs of a population facing severe economic hardship, drought, and displacement. Aid groups say restrictions on female humanitarian workers—who are often essential for reaching women and children in conservative communities—have already hampered relief efforts in several provinces.

Meanwhile, the Taliban's ban on girls attending school beyond the sixth grade remains firmly in place, despite periodic signals from some officials suggesting flexibility might be considered. The restriction, imposed shortly after the group's return to power, has left an estimated 1.4 million girls out of secondary school, according to UNESCO estimates.

At a small school on the outskirts of Kabul, where classrooms that once held teenage girls now sit empty or repurposed, a principal who has worked in education for over two decades described the toll of the policy.

"Every day I see these girls, twelve, thirteen years old, and I have to tell them there is nothing more we can offer them," the principal said. "They ask me when they can come back. I don't have an answer anymore. I used to tell them 'soon,' but it has been years and I cannot lie to them any longer."

The principal, who requested that neither her name nor the school's location be published out of concern for reprisals, said some families have turned to underground schooling networks, though these remain limited, risky, and largely confined to major cities.

"We are losing a generation," she said. "Not because these girls lack the desire to learn—they beg to come back to class—but because of decisions made by men who do not have to look into their faces every morning."

Taliban officials have offered shifting justifications for the ban, at times citing the need to revise curriculum in line with Islamic principles, and at other times suggesting a lack of resources or infrastructure. No timeline for reopening secondary schools to girls has been announced.

Human rights organizations have called the policy a systematic violation of girls' rights to education, with some describing it as a form of gender persecution. The United Nations has repeatedly urged the Taliban to reverse the ban, warning of long-term consequences for the country's health system, economy, and social fabric.

Aid organizations, already navigating the education restrictions in their programming, say the additional pressure on their operations threatens to further destabilize relief efforts heading into the winter months, when needs typically peak.

"We are being squeezed from every direction," the aid coordinator said. "And it is always the most vulnerable—the children, the women—who pay the price."

*Names and identifying details have been withheld or altered in this report to protect sources from potential retaliation.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
